keyPoints: Every Java program starts at public static void main(String[] args) inside a class.
Primitive types (int, double, boolean, char, long) hold values directly; String is a class, not a primitive.
Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 is 3, while 7 / 2.0 is 3.5.

questions.question: What does 7 / 2 evaluate to in Java when both operands are int?
questions.explanation: Integer division discards the fractional part, so 7 / 2 is 3.

questions.question: Which declaration is valid Java?
questions.explanation: An int widens to double automatically. The others mix incompatible types.

questions.question: Which method is the entry point of a Java program?
questions.explanation: The JVM looks for public static void main(String[] args) to start a program.

keyPoints: if/else chooses a branch; switch selects among constants and needs break (or the arrow syntax) to avoid fall-through.
Use for when the number of iterations is known, while when it depends on a condition, and do-while when the body must run at least once.
break leaves the loop; continue skips to the next iteration.

questions.question: Which loop always executes its body at least once?
questions.explanation: do-while checks its condition after the body, so the body runs before the first check.

questions.question: What does continue do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration
questions.explanation: continue jumps to the next iteration; break is the statement that leaves the loop.

questions.question: In an old-style switch, a matching case has no break. What happens?
options: The default case is skipped over
Execution falls through to the next case
questions.explanation: Without break, execution continues into the following case labels until a break or the end.

keyPoints: Java passes arguments by value: a method gets a copy of a primitive, or a copy of an object reference.
Overloading means the same method name with different parameter lists; the return type alone cannot tell overloads apart.
Array indexes start at 0, the last valid index is length - 1, and an array's size is fixed.

questions.question: What is the last valid index of an array with length 5?
questions.explanation: Indexes run from 0 to length - 1, so 0 to 4.

questions.question: Which pair are valid overloads in the same class?
options: int f(int a) and double f(int a)
int f(int a) and int g(int a)
int f(int a) and int f(String a)
questions.explanation: Overloads must differ in their parameter lists. The return type alone is not enough.

questions.question: void inc(int n) { n++; } is called as inc(x) with int x = 5. What is x afterwards?
questions.explanation: Java passes a copy of the value, so the method cannot change the caller's variable.

keyPoints: String objects are immutable: methods such as toUpperCase() return a new String.
Compare String contents with equals(), not ==, which compares references.
Use StringBuilder to build strings in loops; repeated + creates many temporary objects.

questions.question: How should you compare the contents of two Strings a and b?
questions.explanation: equals() compares the characters; == only checks whether both variables point to the same object.

questions.question: What does s.toUpperCase() do to the String s?
options: Returns a new String and leaves s unchanged
Changes the characters of s in place
Throws an exception if s is lowercase
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so the method returns a new String.

questions.question: Which is best for appending thousands of pieces of text in a loop?
questions.explanation: StringBuilder appends into one growing buffer instead of creating a new String every step.

keyPoints: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance created with new, and a constructor initializes it.
Encapsulation: keep fields private and expose behavior through public methods.
static members belong to the class itself, not to any single object.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of making fields private?
options: Encapsulation: control access to the state of an object
Faster execution of every method call
Avoiding the need to write constructors
questions.explanation: Private fields can only change through the class's own methods, which can enforce rules.

questions.question: A static field is shared by...
questions.explanation: There is one copy of a static field, owned by the class.

questions.question: Student a = new Student(); Student b = a; b.name = "Ana"; What is a.name?
questions.explanation: a and b are two references to the same object, so a change through b is visible through a.

keyPoints: A subclass uses extends to inherit fields and methods; super refers to the parent class.
Overriding replaces a parent method in the subclass; the version that runs depends on the real object type (dynamic dispatch).
Every class extends Object, which provides toString(), equals() and hashCode().

questions.question: Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak(); Dog overrides speak(). Which version runs?
questions.explanation: Method calls use the real object type (Dog) at runtime: dynamic dispatch.

questions.question: Which call invokes the parent class constructor?
questions.explanation: super(...) as the first statement of a constructor calls the parent constructor.

questions.question: Which class is the root of every Java class?
questions.explanation: Every class extends java.lang.Object, directly or indirectly.

keyPoints: An interface declares what a type can do; a class implements it and can implement many interfaces.
An abstract class can hold state and partial implementation but cannot be instantiated; a class can extend only one class.
Program to an interface (List<String> x = new ArrayList<>()) so implementations can be swapped.

questions.question: How many classes can a Java class extend directly?
questions.explanation: Java has single class inheritance; multiple interfaces are allowed.

questions.question: Which of these can you NOT do with an abstract class?
questions.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly; only concrete subclasses can.

questions.question: Why write List<String> list = new ArrayList<>() instead of ArrayList<String> list = ...?
options: You can swap the implementation without changing the calling code
It makes the list faster than using ArrayList directly
The compiler refuses ArrayList variables in newer Java
It saves memory because the interface is smaller
questions.explanation: Code that depends on the List interface works with any implementation.

keyPoints: Checked exceptions (such as IOException) must be caught or declared; unchecked ones extend RuntimeException.
finally runs whether or not an exception occurs; try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable resources automatically.
Catch specific exceptions first and never swallow them silently.

questions.question: Which of these is an unchecked exception?
questions.explanation: NullPointerException extends RuntimeException, so it is unchecked.

questions.question: What is try-with-resources used for?
options: Automatically closing resources such as streams
Running code in a new thread
questions.explanation: Resources declared in the try header are closed automatically, even if an exception is thrown.

questions.question: When does a finally block run?
options: Whether or not an exception occurs
Never if there is a catch
questions.explanation: finally runs in both the normal and the exceptional case.

keyPoints: Generics add compile-time type safety: List<String> only holds Strings, so no casts are needed.
A type parameter such as <T> makes a class or method reusable; a bound like <T extends Number> limits it.
List<Integer> is not a List<Number>; use wildcards such as List<? extends Number> to accept both.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of generics?
questions.explanation: The compiler rejects wrong element types and removes the need for casts.

questions.question: What does <T extends Number> mean?
options: T can be Number or any subclass of it
questions.explanation: It is an upper bound: T is Number or a subtype such as Integer or Double.

questions.question: Is a List<Integer> assignable to a List<Number>?
questions.explanation: Generic types are invariant. Use List<? extends Number> to accept lists of subtypes.

keyPoints: List keeps order and allows duplicates; Set rejects duplicates; Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys.
HashMap and HashSet need consistent equals() and hashCode(); lookups are O(1) on average.
ArrayList gives fast index access; LinkedList is better only for frequent insertion and removal at the ends.

questions.question: Which structure maps unique keys to values?
questions.explanation: A Map stores key-value pairs and each key appears once.

questions.question: If two objects are equal by equals(), what must be true of their hashCode()?
options: They must return the same value
hashCode is not used with equals
questions.explanation: The equals/hashCode contract requires equal objects to have equal hash codes.

questions.question: What is the average time to get a value by key from a HashMap?
questions.explanation: Hashing jumps almost directly to the bucket, so lookups are constant time on average.

keyPoints: A lambda is a short implementation of a functional interface (one abstract method), for example x -> x * 2.
Streams process data in a pipeline: a source, intermediate operations (filter, map) and a terminal operation (collect, forEach).
Intermediate stream operations are lazy; nothing runs until a terminal operation is called.

questions.question: Which of these is a terminal stream operation?
questions.explanation: collect ends the pipeline and produces a result; filter, map and sorted are intermediate.

questions.question: What does list.stream().filter(x -> x > 3) return?
options: A Stream of the matching elements
questions.explanation: filter returns another Stream. Nothing runs until a terminal operation is added.

questions.question: What is a functional interface?
options: An interface with exactly one abstract method
An interface with only static methods
questions.explanation: A lambda can implement an interface that has exactly one abstract method.

keyPoints: Threads run concurrently; shared mutable state needs synchronization (synchronized, locks, atomic classes) to avoid race conditions.
Prefer an ExecutorService thread pool to creating threads by hand.
CompletableFuture chains asynchronous steps (supplyAsync, thenApply) without blocking.

questions.question: What is a race condition?
options: A loop that runs slower than expected
Wrong results caused by unsynchronized access to shared data
Two threads each waiting for the other forever
An error the compiler reports for threads
questions.explanation: When threads read and write shared data without coordination, the outcome depends on timing.

questions.question: Which keyword gives a method mutual exclusion?
questions.explanation: synchronized lets only one thread at a time run the method on the same object.

questions.question: Why prefer an ExecutorService over new Thread() for many tasks?
options: Threads cannot be created manually in Java 8+
It forces all tasks to run on a single thread
It removes the need for any synchronization
It reuses a pool of threads and manages their lifecycle
questions.explanation: A pool reuses threads and limits their number, which is cheaper than starting a thread per task.

keyPoints: pwd shows the current folder, ls (dir on Windows) lists files and cd changes folder.
Commands take arguments and flags, for example ls -l.
The output of one command can be piped into another with |, and > redirects output to a file.

questions.question: Which command changes the current directory?
questions.explanation: cd means change directory.

questions.question: What does the | symbol do in a shell?
options: Redirects the output of a command into a file
Feeds the output of one command into the next command
Runs the command in the background
Starts a comment on the rest of the line
questions.explanation: A pipe connects the output of the command on its left to the input of the command on its right.

questions.question: Which command prints the current working directory on Linux and macOS?
questions.explanation: pwd stands for print working directory.

keyPoints: git add stages changes; git commit records a snapshot of the staged changes with a message.
git status shows what changed; git log shows the history.
git push sends commits to a remote such as GitHub; git pull fetches and merges remote changes.

questions.question: Which command records staged changes as a commit?
questions.explanation: git add stages; git commit creates the commit.

questions.question: Which command shows which files are modified or staged?
questions.explanation: git status lists modified, staged and untracked files.

questions.question: What does git push do?
options: Downloads new commits from the remote
Sends local commits to a remote repository
Stages modified files for the next commit
questions.explanation: push uploads your local commits to the remote branch.

keyPoints: A branch is a movable pointer to a line of commits; create one with git switch -c name (or git checkout -b name).
Merging combines branches; a conflict happens when both changed the same lines and must be resolved by hand.
A pull request asks to merge a branch and lets teammates review the change first.

questions.question: When does a merge conflict occur?
options: When the branch name is too long to display
When the repository has no remote configured
When both branches changed the same lines differently
When a commit message is left empty
questions.explanation: Git cannot decide automatically which change to keep, so you resolve it by hand.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a pull request?
options: To download a copy of the repository
To permanently delete an old branch
To create a brand new empty repository
To propose merging a branch and get it reviewed
questions.explanation: A pull request is a reviewable proposal to merge one branch into another.

questions.question: Which command creates a new branch and switches to it?
questions.explanation: git switch -c x creates branch x and checks it out.

keyPoints: Maven uses pom.xml and Gradle uses build.gradle(.kts) to declare dependencies and build steps.
Dependencies are downloaded from repositories such as Maven Central by their coordinates: group, artifact and version.
Typical commands: mvn test and mvn package, or ./gradlew test and ./gradlew build.

questions.question: Which file declares a Maven project's dependencies?
questions.explanation: Maven projects are described by pom.xml.

questions.question: Which command runs the tests of a Gradle project using the wrapper?
questions.explanation: ./gradlew runs the Gradle wrapper; test is the task that runs the tests.

questions.question: What identifies a dependency in Maven?
options: Only its file name on disk
Its file size and checksum only
The license it is published under
questions.explanation: These three coordinates identify exactly one published artifact.

keyPoints: A table has columns and rows; a primary key uniquely identifies each row.
SELECT chooses columns and FROM chooses the table: SELECT name FROM students;
SELECT * returns all columns; in real code list only the columns you need.

questions.question: What does a primary key guarantee?
questions.explanation: A primary key value is unique per row and cannot be NULL.

questions.question: Which query returns only the name column from the students table?
questions.explanation: SQL queries have the form SELECT columns FROM table.

questions.question: What does SELECT * FROM t return?
questions.explanation: The asterisk means every column, and with no WHERE every row.

keyPoints: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY.
Aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) collapse rows into one value per group.
ORDER BY sorts (ascending by default); LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned.

questions.question: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
questions.explanation: WHERE runs before GROUP BY; HAVING filters the resulting groups.

questions.question: What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders return?
options: The number of rows in orders
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows.

questions.question: Which query returns the 3 highest salaries, highest first?
options: SELECT salary FROM emp LIMIT 3 ORDER BY salary;
SELECT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3;
SELECT salary FROM emp GROUP BY 3;
questions.explanation: Sort descending with ORDER BY ... DESC, then keep three rows with LIMIT 3 (in that clause order).

keyPoints: A foreign key links a row to a row in another table.
INNER JOIN returns only matching rows; LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where there is no match.
Always join on key columns (ON a.id = b.a_id); forgetting the condition creates a huge cross product.

questions.question: Which join keeps all rows from the left table even without a match?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills right-side columns with NULL when nothing matches.

questions.question: In a LEFT JOIN, what do right-table columns contain for left rows with no match?
questions.explanation: Missing matches are filled with NULL.

questions.question: What links an orders row to its customer?
options: An index on the orders table
A trigger on the customers table
questions.explanation: A foreign key column in orders references the customer's primary key.

keyPoints: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes rows and DELETE removes rows; always use WHERE with UPDATE and DELETE.
A transaction groups statements: COMMIT saves them all, ROLLBACK undoes them all.
ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability.

questions.question: What does UPDATE employees SET salary = 0; (no WHERE) do?
questions.explanation: Without WHERE the statement applies to all rows in the table.

questions.question: What does ROLLBACK do?
options: Undoes the changes of the current transaction
Deletes the table from the database
Locks the table for other users
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK discards all changes made since the transaction began.

questions.question: In ACID, what does Atomicity mean?
options: Stored data is encrypted on disk
A transaction happens completely or not at all
Queries always finish in constant time
Every table must have a primary key
questions.explanation: Atomic means all-or-nothing.

keyPoints: One-to-many is modelled with a foreign key on the 'many' side; many-to-many needs a join table.
First normal form: atomic values and no repeating groups. Second and third forms remove partial and transitive dependencies.
Normalization reduces duplication and update anomalies; denormalizing can help read speed.

questions.question: How do you model a many-to-many relationship between students and courses?
options: A join table with foreign keys to both
questions.explanation: A join table (for example enrollments) holds one row per student-course pair.

questions.question: What does normalization mainly reduce?
questions.explanation: Storing each fact once avoids inconsistent copies.

questions.question: One author has many books. Where does the foreign key go?
questions.explanation: The foreign key goes on the 'many' side, so each book row stores its author's id.

keyPoints: An index (often a B-tree) lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.
Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY; each index slows INSERT and UPDATE and uses space.
EXPLAIN shows the query plan, for example whether a full table scan or an index scan is used.

questions.question: What is the main cost of adding many indexes?
questions.explanation: Every insert or update must also maintain each index.

questions.question: Which keyword shows how the database will execute a query?
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN prints the query plan.

questions.question: A query filters WHERE email = 'a@b.com' on a huge table. What helps most?
questions.explanation: An index on the filtered column avoids scanning every row.

keyPoints: A Connection opens a session to the database; a Statement runs SQL; a ResultSet iterates over returned rows with next().
Use PreparedStatement with ? placeholders to prevent SQL injection instead of concatenating strings.
Close connections with try-with-resources and map each row to an object by reading columns by name.

questions.question: Why use PreparedStatement instead of building SQL with string concatenation?
options: It prevents SQL injection by separating SQL from values
It is the only way to run SQL from Java
It avoids having to open a connection
It keeps every ResultSet in memory forever
questions.explanation: Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so user input cannot change the query.

questions.question: How do you move to the next row of a ResultSet?
questions.explanation: next() advances the cursor and returns false when there are no more rows.

questions.question: How should JDBC resources be closed safely?
options: Never; the garbage collector does it
questions.explanation: try-with-resources closes the ResultSet, Statement and Connection even when exceptions occur.

keyPoints: A client sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body); the server returns a response (status code, headers, body).
GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part of a resource and DELETE removes it.
Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

questions.question: Which status code means the requested resource was not found?
questions.explanation: 404 Not Found.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is normally used to read data without side effects?
questions.explanation: GET is safe: it only retrieves data.

questions.question: A 5xx status code indicates...
questions.explanation: 5xx means the server failed to handle a valid request.

keyPoints: REST models things as resources with nouns in URLs (/students/42) and uses HTTP methods as the actions.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating the request leaves the same result; POST is not.
Use meaningful status codes: 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found.

questions.question: Which request is best REST style for deleting student 42?
questions.explanation: The URL names the resource and the HTTP method says what to do with it.

questions.question: Which method is NOT idempotent?
questions.explanation: Repeating a POST can create several resources.

questions.question: Which status code fits a successful creation of a resource?
questions.explanation: 201 Created tells the client a new resource now exists.

keyPoints: JSON has objects {}, arrays [], strings, numbers, booleans and null; keys are double-quoted strings.
Jackson's ObjectMapper converts Java objects to JSON (writeValueAsString) and back (readValue).
Annotations such as @JsonProperty and @JsonIgnore customize field names and visibility.

questions.question: Which Jackson class converts between JSON and Java objects?
questions.explanation: ObjectMapper is Jackson's main entry point (Gson is a different library).

questions.question: Which of these is valid JSON?
questions.explanation: JSON keys and string values must use double quotes.

questions.question: What does @JsonIgnore do on a field?
options: Makes the field required in the JSON
Renames the field in the JSON
Encrypts the value of the field
Excludes it from JSON output and input
questions.explanation: The field is skipped when serializing and deserializing.

keyPoints: Inversion of control: the Spring container creates objects (beans) and wires their dependencies for you.
Prefer constructor injection: dependencies are explicit, can be final and are easy to test.
@Component, @Service and @Repository mark classes as beans; @Bean in a @Configuration class defines beans in code.

questions.question: What is a Spring bean?
options: An object managed by the Spring container
Any ordinary Java object you create
A single row stored in a database
A configuration file in the project
questions.explanation: Beans are the objects the container creates, configures and injects.

questions.question: Which injection style is generally preferred?
questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and testable.

questions.question: Which annotation marks a class as a business-logic bean?
questions.explanation: @Service is a stereotype annotation for service-layer beans.

keyPoints: Starters (for example spring-boot-starter-web) bring a set of compatible dependencies.
Auto-configuration configures beans based on the classpath and your properties.
@SpringBootApplication enables component scanning and auto-configuration; settings live in application.properties or application.yml.

questions.question: What does @SpringBootApplication enable?
questions.explanation: It combines @Configuration, @ComponentScan and @EnableAutoConfiguration.

questions.question: Where would you normally set server.port?
questions.explanation: Boot reads settings such as server.port from application.properties or application.yml.

questions.question: What is a Spring Boot starter dependency?
options: A curated group of dependencies for a feature
A plugin that starts the JVM
questions.explanation: A starter pulls in all the libraries needed for a feature, such as web or JPA.

keyPoints: @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, so return values become the response body (as JSON).
@GetMapping and @PostMapping map URLs; @PathVariable reads /students/{id}, @RequestParam reads ?name= and @RequestBody reads the JSON body.
ResponseEntity lets you control the status code and headers.

questions.question: Which annotation reads the id from the URL /students/{id}?
questions.explanation: @PathVariable binds a URL path segment to a method parameter.

questions.question: Which annotation binds a JSON request body to a Java object?
questions.explanation: @RequestBody deserializes the HTTP body, typically JSON, into the parameter.

questions.question: What does @RestController add compared to @Controller?
questions.explanation: Return values are written straight to the response body instead of being treated as view names.

keyPoints: @Entity maps a class to a table and @Id marks the primary key.
A JpaRepository<T, ID> interface gives CRUD methods without writing implementations; derived queries such as findByEmail are generated from the method name.
@Transactional makes a method run in one transaction; lazy relationships load on first access.

questions.question: Which interface gives you ready-made CRUD methods for an entity?
questions.explanation: Extending JpaRepository gives save, findById, findAll, delete and more.

questions.question: What does declaring findByEmail(String email) in a repository do?
options: It must be implemented by hand
Spring generates a query filtering by email
questions.explanation: Spring Data parses the method name and builds the query for you.

questions.question: Which annotation marks the primary key field of an entity?
questions.explanation: @Id identifies the primary key attribute.

keyPoints: Bean Validation annotations such as @NotBlank, @Size, @Email and @Min go on fields and are triggered by @Valid on the request body.
@ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler centralizes error handling for all controllers.
Return a consistent error body (status, message, field errors) with a proper status such as 400 or 404.

questions.question: Which annotation on a parameter triggers validation of a request body?
questions.explanation: @Valid tells Spring to validate the object using its constraint annotations.

questions.question: What does @ControllerAdvice allow?
options: Running SQL queries against the database
questions.explanation: Handlers declared there apply to every controller.

questions.question: Which status code fits a request with invalid input?
questions.explanation: 400 Bad Request means the client sent something invalid.

keyPoints: Authentication verifies who you are; authorization decides what you may do.
Never store plain-text passwords; hash them with a slow, salted algorithm such as BCrypt.
A SecurityFilterChain bean configures which endpoints need authentication or specific roles.

questions.question: What is authorization?
options: Deciding what a logged-in user may access
questions.explanation: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides permissions.

questions.question: How should passwords be stored?
options: Hashed with a salted algorithm such as BCrypt
Encrypted with a key kept in the code
questions.explanation: A slow salted hash makes stolen databases hard to crack.

questions.question: Which bean defines which endpoints require login?
questions.explanation: A SecurityFilterChain bean configures request authorization rules.

keyPoints: A JUnit 5 test is a method annotated with @Test; it passes unless an assertion fails or an exception is thrown.
Common assertions: assertEquals(expected, actual), assertTrue and assertThrows.
@BeforeEach runs before every test; @ParameterizedTest runs one test with many inputs.

questions.question: In assertEquals(a, b), which value should come first?
options: Either; the compiler enforces the order
The first argument must be null
questions.explanation: By convention the expected value comes first so failure messages read correctly.

questions.question: Which annotation runs a method before every test?
questions.explanation: @BeforeEach runs before each test method.

questions.question: How do you check that code throws an exception in JUnit 5?
questions.explanation: assertThrows(Type.class, () -> code) passes only if that exception is thrown.

keyPoints: A mock replaces a real dependency so a class can be tested in isolation.
when(mock.method()).thenReturn(value) stubs behavior; verify(mock).method() checks that an interaction happened.
Mock collaborators such as repositories and clients, not the class under test or simple value objects.

questions.question: What does when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(x) do?
options: Makes the mock return x for that call
questions.explanation: It stubs the mock so findById(1L) returns x.

questions.question: Which call checks that a mock's method was invoked?
questions.explanation: verify(mock).method() fails the test if the call did not happen.

questions.question: What is the main reason to mock a repository in a unit test?
options: To make the test run more slowly
To test the database engine itself
To test the service without a real database
questions.explanation: Mocks keep unit tests fast and isolated from external systems.

keyPoints: @SpringBootTest starts the full application context; it is slow, so use it sparingly.
MockMvc sends simulated HTTP requests to controllers; @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer and @DataJpaTest only the persistence layer.
Use @MockBean (or @MockitoBean in newer Spring versions) to replace beans in a test slice.

questions.question: Which annotation loads only the web layer for controller tests?
questions.explanation: @WebMvcTest is a test slice limited to controllers and web configuration.

questions.question: What is MockMvc used for?
options: Mocking the database layer for tests
Sending simulated HTTP requests to controllers
Running the app in a production profile
questions.explanation: MockMvc exercises controllers without starting a real server.

questions.question: Why use test slices instead of @SpringBootTest everywhere?
options: They start faster by loading less
They always use a real server
questions.explanation: Loading only the needed layer makes tests much faster.
